Huang resignation · dated public records, Nov 2026 · draft

Fifteen days, mapped: the coverage, who acted, and the documented ties

Top right, each dot is one piece on the story. Below it, each row is one actor and each chip one dated act. At left, each line is a documented tie between an actor and a company, a funder or a group: a contribution, a post held, a grant, an official act. Both slices repeat the same companies, funders and people at their left; a dashed box names an actor whose own row is in another slice. The ties are mapped outward from Anthropic and Open Philanthropy; Nvidia's are added where the same kind of record was searched (the note at the foot lists them), and each group's heading gives the rule for who is drawn. The figure sets these records side by side; it does not say one caused another.

THREE NEWSPAPERS
Background: The New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times cover chips and China.
No document here shows who their confidential intelligence sources are. Singapore's ministry denied the Journal's Oct 30 account in a statement timed the same day.
BYLINES WITH A TIE ON RECORD
No document here shows whether a tie shaped any of the five pieces. All 888 names in the bylines of the saved pages were looked up; five have a tie on record (three of them to the Tarbell Center). A reporter or columnist without one is not drawn, however often quoted.
ANALYSTS QUOTED OR POSTING
Background: Chris McGuire, now at the Council on Foreign Relations, "crafted and implemented" the Biden administration's chip export controls at the NSC, his biography says. CNAS published on chip smuggling in 2025.
No document here shows who, if anyone, prompted the posts or quotes. Drawn: 16 of the 282 analysts, experts and research groups quoted: those with a tie on record to Anthropic, Open Philanthropy or Nvidia, their own or through the organisation where they hold a post.
SENATE
Background: Democrats sen. Schumer was an original cosponsor of the GAIN AI Act on chip exports.
No document here shows any contact between a senator and the reporters or their sources.
HOUSE
Background: Rep. Mast's AI OVERWATCH Act, which would let Congress block advanced chip exports, passed his committee in January.
No document here shows whether anyone outside Congress had a hand in the Nov 4 letter.
THE ADMINISTRATION
Background: The government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip for sale to China this year. As CNBC relays the Times's reporting, policymakers received the intelligence memo last spring and Trump, once briefed, "chose not to do anything."
No document here shows who gave the intelligence to reporters. The reports cite "people briefed on intelligence surveillance."
The New York Times what it reported, from its own pages unless a chip says otherwise
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
U.S. intelligence surveilled Alice Huang; its first report says that "Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings" and "chose not to do anything with the information", and that the Commerce Department's investigation of Megaspeed "was handed over this year to the Justice Department". Of Huang it says that when the president was first briefed "U.S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Ms. Huang was gathering information for the Chinese", that "It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment", and that "some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Mr. Huang could have remained unaware" of the role they had concluded she had. It dates that investigation to "late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious", the Nvidia equipment "still packed in boxes"; and says that Singapore "has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed" and that in 2025 its authorities "brought Ms. Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her". It recalls photographs "posted to LinkedIn" in June 2024, "just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases", that "showed Mr. Huang alongside Ms. Huang at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show", and that in May 2025 "they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other A.I. suppliers"; "Those details were described in a Times article last October", it says (the company's explanations of the photographs are on its chips of Oct 31 and Nov 9)
Reports, in its article on the chairmen's letter, that Sen. Warren "renewed her call for testimony" the week before, after its first report; Huang had turned down her request in June to appear before the Senate
A memo says China's spy agency recruited her
Reports that the Commerce Department "has approved dozens of Chinese companies to handle Nvidia's H200 chips, some of which have ties to firms under sanctions over national security". It says the administration "approved this Chinese firm to assemble Nvidia's advanced chips into the computers that create artificial intelligence", though its listed address "stands empty" and "there is little evidence the firm actually exists"; its owners have ties to a "Chinese private equity fund that the U.S. government placed on a trade blacklist in 2024", and two analysts "said they believed New Matrix may be a front for firms associated with that fund"; it "is the second Chinese company approved to handle Nvidia's H200 chips that does not seem to have any physical presence at its listed address". It adds that "several other Chinese companies approved to purchase H200 chips or assemble them into servers have ties to firms that have been blacklisted by the U.S. government, or that work as military contractors in China", and that the department "appears to have approved roughly two dozen Chinese firms to buy or handle" the chips. The paper also says that "Nvidia is now selling only small amounts of H200 chips to China" and that the firms "have not yet met that quota". The saved copy of the Times's page was updated on Nov 8; the Jerusalem Post relays these findings on Nov 7. The replies of the export bureau and of Nvidia are their chips of that day. Recalls, in its report on licences for chip sales to Chinese firms, what Nvidia disclosed for its summer quarter: "In the quarter that ended in July, H200 shipments to customers based in China made up less than 1 percent of Nvidia's revenue from data centers", and "The company also said in August that it was not assuming any sales to China in its estimate for data center revenue for the current quarter". The saved copy of the Times's page was updated on Nov 8; the Jerusalem Post relays both sentences on Nov 7, as "Nvidia's financial disclosures cited by NYT". Unite.AI, on Nov 5, in an article that does not mention the affair, had described the quarterly report for the period that ended July 26 in like terms: licences from February 2026 "allowed small amounts of H200 products to be shipped to specific China-based customers", the shipments made "represented less than 1% of Data Center revenue in the quarter covered by the report", the company "assessed that it was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data-center computing market" without approval from both governments, and it "had been unable to pass any of the tariff to customers". A wire sentence words the disclosure: "Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Beijing government". It stands in RTÉ's page, first published on the evening of Nov 8 and updated on Nov 9; no first-day version of that page is saved, so the sentence may be newer than Nov 8 (a copy of the same article timed the next morning lacks it), and the Associated Press's dispatch of Nov 9 has it but for one word. The filing itself is saved, the company's quarterly report for the period that ended July 26: licences "would allow us to ship small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, but such sales were restricted by the PRC government", and "Those shipments account for less than 1% of Data Center revenue in our most recent quarter"
Rubio oversaw the memo. Its report: the secretary of state "oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials" of Huang's relationship, according to "multiple people briefed on the matter", and the memo "was circulated to administration officials with high-level security clearances ahead of a trip Mr. Trump took to China in May". Reports that Nvidia opened its inquiry after Huang "acknowledged to the company's board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy" (as Boston.com carries the article)
Reports that a Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed "came to a sudden halt late last year" and was "transferred to the Justice Department", after Nvidia's general counsel emailed the investigators in August 2025. It says the transfer was "to avoid any potential compromise" of the investigation, that Justice "is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed", and that "it is not clear if other factors contributed". After the email, it says, Commerce officials "rapidly disclosed it to partner law enforcement agencies", and "The Justice Department requested that the Commerce Department pause its work on the investigation, and Commerce complied, one person familiar with the case said"; the outcome, it adds, "was a source of frustration to agents investigating Megaspeed, who had spent months building a case". Of the email it reports, from people familiar with the incident and a Commerce official: he told the agents the under secretary had given him permission to reach out about the case; Nvidia had asked them directly for a meeting with one of them, and when they turned it down he replied that he was unsure what the issue was, because the under secretary had said Nvidia could communicate with the bureau's employees. It adds that the investigators forwarded the email chain to the under secretary, and that since the president's return to office he and other leaders of the department "had mandated that any investigations into Nvidia and other outreach to the company first receive their approval"
Reports that the president was told aboard Air Force One in May, by Rubio, of the intelligence on Huang, which "contradicts the president's assertion" that he had not known then; the White House "disputed the reporting", it says, "without elaborating". Reports, in a profile of Alice Huang, that in 2024 "Taiwanese authorities began to monitor Ms. Huang's trips to the island at the suggestion of the U.S. government", citing a person familiar with the matter (as Business Standard carries the article). The profile also reports that Megaspeed "was named a Nvidia cloud partner" four days after a change of its ownership (the Journal's profile of the day before dates the partnership by a letter of November 2023: the Journal's act of Nov 9), and repeats, from the Times's first report (its act of Oct 29), that in late 2024 the Commerce Department "sent an official to inspect a Megaspeed data center", where "Some Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes". It also reports, from a person familiar with the investigation, that Singapore "prohibited Ms. Huang from leaving the country and brought her in for questioning in 2025 as part of an investigation into false declaration of imports", and that "There was insufficient evidence to suggest that Ms. Huang was complicit in the false declarations and investigations against her were concluded" (Singapore's own statement followed on Nov 12)
A second relationship, with a subordinate. Reports that Bessent "confronted" Lutnick at the White House over Megaspeed, as "described by people briefed on it"; a Commerce spokeswoman denies the conversation took place; it adds that the move to blacklist Megaspeed had earlier come before a meeting of cabinet deputies, where a Commerce under secretary "deferred on taking action, saying that the decision was up to Mr. Lutnick"
Recalls, in a profile of the interim chief (as the San Francisco Examiner carries it), that as chief financial officer she "expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China": "In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20% to 25% of the company's data center revenue"
The Wall Street Journal what it reported, from its own page saved by hand and from copies its licensed partners carry
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
Reports that officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan "have grown concerned" that an executive close to Huang "is a Chinese intelligence source", citing people familiar with the matter (Singapore denied the account in a statement timed the same day). It says authorities in Singapore and Taiwan "had separately investigated Alice Huang's ties to China, at one point putting physical surveillance teams on her", and that a Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, begun in late 2024, "largely stalled", with the Justice Department "now leading the probe". It quotes Megaspeed's statement of late 2025 that reviews "confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities", and recalls the arrest in March of a co-founder of the server maker Super Micro "on charges of violating U.S. export-control laws"; Super Micro, it adds, said then that it was cooperating with investigators and Nvidia that "compliance with export restrictions is a top priority"; both companies "denied wrongdoing at the time", and he pleaded not guilty
Reports, in an article on who could succeed Huang, that Nvidia's latest proxy statement warns it is "highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team" and that a failure to ensure effective succession planning could "hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success". Reports, in a profile of Alice Huang (as To Vima and a licensed Dow Jones copy carry the article), that "According to a November 2023 letter posted on its website, Megaspeed became a member of an Nvidia partnership program, a status that typically grants priority access to the latest chips". Its editorial board writes the same day that Megaspeed "was then sold to a Singapore-based shell company in November 2023", and that Nvidia made it a cloud partner "Soon afterward". The Times's profile of the next day puts the designation four days after the change of ownership (the Times's act of Nov 10)
Reports that the board "is preparing to oust" Huang and "to meet as soon as today to determine his future", citing people familiar with the matter. Reports, in a Heard on the Street column that evening, that Nvidia stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore, 22% of its revenue until then, in the quarter after it blocked Megaspeed: from the quarter that ended in October 2025 it reported revenue by "the location of the customers' headquarters" and no longer by "customer billing location". "It isn't clear if the two are related", the column says. It quotes the filing: the change "provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue", since billing locations "often reflected a customer's centralized invoicing location, even though our products were almost always shipped elsewhere"; and the filing of a quarter before: "customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere"
Financial Times what it reported, from its own page
Its report of Sep 4, 2025 that Anthropic would stop selling AI services to groups majority-owned by Chinese entities cited "an Anthropic executive familiar with the matter", as Bloomberg Law relays it. No record here shows who the sources of its Nov 6 report were
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
Reports that the U.S. government "believes" Huang "had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China's main intelligence agency", citing people familiar with the matter. It says a memo by U.S. officials stating this "was shared with a small group of top US officials shortly before" the president flew to Beijing; that sentence stands in a copy of the page updated on Nov 7, and the report's earlier saved forms (an archived opening and its reporter's post of Nov 6) do not reach it, so it may be newer than the report's first day. The first saved page that has the president himself notified is a relay of the next day (the FT's row, Nov 7). Its reporter's post of the report: 3.4M views. Reports that before the president's trip to China in May, when he learnt that Huang was not in the group, he called him, and Huang flew to Alaska, where he boarded the presidential jet during a stopover
Engadget, relaying the FT's report of the day before, writes that the president, "along with select American officials, were notified about it before his trip to Beijing earlier this year", and that he "reportedly took no action about that information". It is the first saved page that has the president himself notified; the saved copy of the FT's own report says the memo went to "a small group of top US officials" (its act of Nov 6), and the FT writes on Nov 9 that it had reported the president was briefed (its act of Nov 9)
Writes, in its report of the president's remarks that day, that it "previously reported that the president was briefed in May on a top-secret memo that included information about the affair"; its report of Nov 6, as saved, says the memo "was shared with a small group of top US officials shortly before" his flight to Beijing. In the same sentence it has the president saying he "had been informed about Huang's situation only recently", and it prints his reply when asked about the memo: "I'd certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned" (his act of that day). The Times reports a briefing aboard the plane the next day (the Times's act of Nov 10). Reports, from "two investors pitched on the deal", that in early 2025 an executive of Megaspeed and her business partner sought investment for a "south-east Asia data centre project worth several hundred million dollars": the pair "said they had" what one investor quotes as "no problem securing GPUs" and "cited Alibaba as a client of the project, according to one investor present". It adds that she "did not disclose any close relationship with Nvidia's chief executive" in the pitch; that "The allegation of espionage could not be independently verified by the FT"; that of the photographs of the two "None of the photos suggest inappropriate relationships and several are in a group setting"; that Megaspeed has "strongly denied allegations of any illicit activity involving chips"; and, from company documents, that Alibaba, through a Singaporean subsidiary, lent money to a Malaysian subsidiary of Megaspeed in June 2024. It says neither the executive nor her partner could be reached, and that Alibaba "did not immediately respond to a request for comment"
Reports that the Commerce Department "sought over the past two months to delay new inclusions" on the entity list ("one of the people said"), its officials saying they needed more information about some companies; the paper adds: "It was unclear if Megaspeed was one of the companies, but the delay has meant it remains off the entity list". It reports, from people familiar with the matter, that the state, energy and Treasury departments and the Pentagon "were among the agencies that were pushing for Megaspeed's inclusion on the list". Reports, in its piece "Too big to fire", that Megaspeed, according to that company's documents, "has been the recipient of loans from the US chip group in 2024"

Publishes "Jensen Huang should resign": "An investigation is necessary to see just how bad the incident was", but "its findings are not needed to decide what to do with Jensen, who in recent weeks appears to have misled his own employees, investors and the public"; "even if Alice Huang is an ordinary civilian, the affair and events surrounding it are unacceptable for a CEO of a major company"; "in recent weeks Nvidia and Huang have issued multiple statements we now know to be false". "In the worst case, Nvidia may have fundamentally undermined American national security and AI leadership"; "we do not know if the affair was disclosed to Nvidia's board or if Huang removed himself from decision-making involving Megaspeed"; it does not know whether the company's spokesman knew his statements were false ("if not, Huang appears to have misled his own executives as well"); "Nvidia's board may keep him around"
Zvi Mowshowitz author of a newsletter on AI
The Survival and Flourishing Fund lists a $200,000 "unconditional gift" to him in 2024 from Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic's first funding round in 2021; he has written of serving as a recommender for that fund. No record here ties the gift to this piece
In his weekly newsletter, on the Times report: "you should be entirely unshocked that such a spy is out there"; "this is me not updating"; and he goes on: "Nor am I updating on the rest of the story, about how Nvidia has managed to compromise the White House, largely through flattery, and how when the White House noticed a Chinese spy it did not announce this fact"
Publishes "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had an Affair With a Chinese Spy": "National security has been compromised. He must resign"; "I would be very surprised if Jensen Huang knew he was being compromised by a Chinese agent"; he accepts as "a mitigating factor" that Huang "was up against actual professional spies and an active operation to compromise him"; "If he will not resign, the board must remove him. If the board will not remove him, the United States Government should force him to step down"; and anyone in the government "who knowingly let this go on for a year should be offering their resignation as well". He also writes that the affair "is not necessary to explain" Huang's conduct on chip sales to China: "He might or might not have done that anyway, or done that to the same extent"
In his weekly newsletter, "Spy Versus Guy": removing Huang "will be tricky because Jensen Huang deliberately tried to make himself unfireable, with over 50 direct reports and no succession plan"

His podcast releases two episodes: an "emergency pod", "Jensen and His Spy", with Chris McGuire, and one recorded, it says, "Friday afternoon, before the FT reported", with a part on "the alleged spy in Jensen Huang's orbit". The recordings were not heard

Ryan Fedasiuk Foundation for American Innovation
CSET at Georgetown: listed as research analyst, 2019–22 rosters
Open Philanthropy made three awards to his institution, the Foundation for American Innovation: $976,000 for AI policy in 2023–24 (the second an exit grant) and $2.7M for energy permitting in 2026. No record here ties an award to him
Tells the Journal: "It was this unparalleled access to politicos and other industry titans that made him such an attractive target for Chinese intelligence to begin with". Posts that morning, on the Times's report: "it appears Nvidia executive leadership personally reached out to the Commerce Department in an effort to get it to drop its investigation into Megaspeed"; "I am not an investor, but at first look, this would appear to be a gross violation of Mr. Huang's fiduciary responsibility as CEO", and "a textbook example of (FAILED!) attempted political corruption by one of America's largest tech companies"; he asks that "Any independent investigation into Mr. Huang's personal affair must get to the bottom of whether Nvidia's efforts to protect Megaspeed were ultimately influenced by that relationship"; and: "If Nvidia thought it could persuade the Trump administration to drop its investigation into Mr. Huang's girlfriend, then that is a total betrayal of President Trump's trust". In a second post that afternoon he quotes Bloomberg: the company's tabulations "undercounted the number of chips it had sold to Megaspeed via hardware partners by 50,000 units, according to trade records analyzed by Bloomberg"
A podcast episode titled "Jensen Huang Must Resign" is released. The day is the release time in the data of a summary page that prints no date; the recording was not heard. The page's summary has him say that whether sensitive information reached Chinese intelligence is unknown ("we really don't know anything about" the nature of the relationship), and of the motive he alleges: "I'm reading between the lines"
Tells Scientific American Huang is in "almost every aspect of the company"; writes at his institute's site that it is "a sad day for Nvidia", that "there is reason to be optimistic" about the company and that stepping down "was dignified, and ultimately the right decision". Also to Scientific American: "The longer this drags on", "the more distracted the company will grow"; and "I don't think it's right to conceive of this as 'if Jensen goes, then there goes a huge blow to the company's technical capability'". His piece ends: "gratitude does not excuse Huang's personal misconduct", nor should admiration for him or blame over the scandal "obscure deeper problems in his company's conduct". Tells the Washington Post, of accounts defending Huang: "There are many actors in the American economy who believe that Mr. Huang's personal status as CEO of the company is an essential part of American economic growth"
Chris McGuire Council on Foreign Relations
NSC technology office: deputy senior director, 2022–24
Tarun Chhabra: scheduled for the same session, Taipei, Jun 6, 2026
The Council on Foreign Relations lists Nvidia among its corporate members, in its Bronze tier, as of Sep 3, 2026
Recap post asks why Commerce took no action. 9.4M views. Posts that afternoon, on the Times's report of the day: "the best evidence is the fact that the MSS is actively trying to convince us to loosen them!"; "Nvidia's most advanced chips remain available to Megaspeed"; "And for some reason, @BISgov refuses to cut them off". A newsletter of Nov 10 quotes the post; until Nov 17 this chip stood on that day
Post: "Jensen's behavior is only half the story"; "Obviously Nvidia needs to take significant steps in its operations, security, and policy advocacy to ensure it takes national security concerns more seriously". In the same post: "The biggest problem remains unaddressed"; "it is even more important that the Department of Commerce tighten up export controls to prevent things like this from ever happening again". Posts that Sunday: "So Rubio himself is worried about Jensen's romantic relationship with the Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, meaning the intel was validated at the highest levels of government. But still, Commerce has done nothing to limit AI chip shipments to Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. Why?" (The National embeds the post in its report of Nov 9)
Tells Bloomberg, as The National relays it: "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him - it really needs to be looked into". Posts, on the Times's report of that day: "It is beyond inappropriate that leadership at the Department of Commerce apparently discussed an ongoing law enforcement investigation involving Megaspeed and Nvidia with Nvidia's General Counsel"; "It's clear that Congressional oversight is urgently needed here"; "Law enforcement agencies (which include the Department of Commerce) cannot discuss ongoing investigations, and particularly not with companies directly or indirectly involved with cases"; and Congress "should immediately pass the many bipartisan bills that would tighten export controls and that are currently pending, such as the AI Overwatch Act, MATCH Act, Chip Security Act". Of the department he writes that "Commerce has shielded Megaspeed from regulatory action at every turn, and may have shielded Megaspeed from legal action as well", that it "is refusing to enforce EXISTING U.S. export controls", and that it "should: (1) immediately enforce the existing export control regulations that would require licenses for large AI chip shipments to non-trusted entities in Southeast Asia and other countries, such as Megaspeed; and (2) close obviously loopholes in controls that permit companies like Megaspeed to provide remote access of AI chips to China", or let subsidiaries of listed Chinese companies "buy AI chips in the United States"
Tells the FT, for its report on the delayed listing of Megaspeed: "It is mind-boggling that commerce knew months ago that Megaspeed is being run by a Chinese spy but did nothing to stop them from buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips"; "I can't come up with a single good reason for that inaction". The FT adds that he said the department "should take steps to prevent any untrusted companies such as Megaspeed from buying AI chips without an export licence, which he said was required under existing export-control rules"; guest on the ChinaTalk podcast. In a piece of the Council on Foreign Relations, where he is a fellow: Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention"; of rules that would require licences, "the Department of Commerce is refusing to enforce them"; it should "impose new controls that ban Chinese companies from renting remote access to the AI chips that they are currently prohibited from purchasing". Tells the Journal, of the chip-export bills: "They should just be pushed now and voted on, up or down, as a way to signal Congress's concern about this issue and how it's being handled"
Tells the Washington Post by email that he had "definitely" noticed the accounts that targeted his posts, and had assumed they were Chinese bot accounts. The New York Post, as AOL carries it, has him call the Commerce Department's handling of the Megaspeed matter "stunning", and quotes him: "The president has been pretty clear - no Blackwells to China"; "And the way that Commerce is implementing export controls is massively undermining the president's policy". CBS News quotes him: "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls"; it has him add that the department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was run by a woman the U.S. believes to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing"; and: "Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang". CBS says the department "did not respond to a request for comment". The saved copy of CBS's page was changed on Nov 13; ANI carries the first sentence that evening, U.S. Eastern time, and no saved page of Nov 12 carries the last

In an article of his own on The Substrate: "Together, smuggling and remote access probably account for almost half of the compute China has access to, more than its own AI chip industry has produced"; he calls the estimates he uses "highly uncertain" and says that varying one of them "moves the combined share between about 36% and 61%". Of the company: "NVIDIA has done more to stop smuggling in 2026", "But one might fairly ask why NVIDIA didn't do this in 2024 or 2025, when there were already many credible reports of smuggling and NVIDIA was saying there was no evidence of it". Of the board's inquiry: "It remains to be seen how impartial and thorough that investigation will be". Anthropic's own lobbying report for the third quarter of 2026 lists, among the measures it lobbied on, "S.5105 - Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act" and "S.Amdt.6561 to S.4784; provisions related to Artificial Intelligence". The bill is Sen. Schiff's, with Sen. Banks as its cosponsor, introduced on July 23, 2026: "A bill to establish the applicability of antitrust laws to the sharing of artificial intelligence frontier model risks, and for other purposes"; it was referred to the Judiciary Committee. The amendment, to the defense authorization bill for fiscal 2027, was submitted on July 13 by Sen. Schiff "(for himself and Mr. Banks)" and "ordered to lie on the table". Its text: "It shall not be considered a violation of any provision of the antitrust laws for" two or more non-Federal entities "to provide or exchange information or assistance relating to a covered artificial intelligence security risk in good faith for the exclusive purpose of a covered artificial intelligence security purpose" (protecting against, testing or mitigating such a risk; the risks it lists are help with chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or offensive cyber weapons, loss of control over critical infrastructure, AI that escapes oversight or improves itself, theft or use by an adversary nation, and unauthorized access, which includes "systematic querying or automated extraction designed to distill, replicate, or reconstruct model capabilities"), or to do so "for the exclusive purpose of coordinating strategies to reduce covered artificial intelligence security risks via delaying or otherwise limiting the release, deployment, use, development, training, testing, or evaluation of artificial intelligence, provided that the non-Federal entities submit prior written notice of the proposed coordinated delay or limitation to the Attorney General, detailing the specific covered artificial intelligence security risk and the scope of the proposed restriction". Its conditions and limits: "exclusive purpose" means "with not more than an insubstantial part of the information or assistance being for other purposes"; an entity that receives information is covered only if it "uses such information or assistance for a covered artificial intelligence security purpose and has implemented reasonable internal controls"; the first clause "shall not be construed to permit price-fixing, allocating a market between competitors, monopolizing or attempting to monopolize a market, boycotting, or exchanges of price or cost information"; the exemption "shall constitute an affirmative defense", and the entity claiming it "shall bear the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the entity's actions were taken in good faith and for the exclusive purpose described"; "The Attorney General may seek" an injunction where he determines that the entities "are not acting in good faith or are otherwise unreasonably engaging in anticompetitive acts" (the text asks for notice to him, not for his approval); and nothing in it limits "any private right of action for any violation of the antitrust laws that is not exempt". A lobbying report names the measures lobbied on and no position: whether the company supported, opposed or sought changes to either, and on which provision, the report does not say. The same report names other measures on the rules for AI, again with no position, among them "H.R.7688 - DPA Modernization Act of 2026", "H.R.9925 - FRONTIER Act", "S.5061 - Secure A.I. Development Act of 2026", "S.5252 - BLADE Act", "Executive Order 14409 - Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security", "Executive Order 14434 - Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence" and "BIS-2025-0001: Artificial Intelligence Diffusion Rule and Export Controls"; what each provides is not read here. Neither the bill nor the amendment is one of the five chip-export measures that the lines on lobbying reports count

Letter with Sen. Wyden opens a probe of chip-export approvals; it says the administration "did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat"; it asks the department to preserve all records of its tariff investigation of semiconductors, of Nvidia's export licence applications and of its communications with and about Nvidia and Huang. The letter calls the tariff collected on the chips "what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system", says the department approved sales to Chinese companies "with government and military ties", and says: "There appears to be a profound lack of due diligence in Commerce's process for approving these Chinese buyers of Nvidia chips". It says the president's approval of the H200 exports, "apparently granted with knowledge of Mr. Huang's compromised position and only after Mr. Huang and Nvidia directed at least $26 million toward President Trump's personal priorities such as the White House ballroom", "raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration"; that his use of the tariff statute "appears to have done the opposite, undermining U.S. national security and putting Americans at risk"; and the records it asks for include "the report you allegedly transmitted to the President on December 22, 2025"

On Sept 29, 2026 its chief executive signed, with the president and five other companies, the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (what follows is the figure's one account of the accord, for OpenAI as for Anthropic: OpenAI's line points to it): by Axios (Sep 30), it was "signed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia" (whose chief executive then, Axios adds, was "seated beside Trump" and "supplied the day's credo", which it quotes: "Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned") and "formalizes industry self-regulation as Washington's response to the most alarming run of AI safety failures yet"; the president called it "morally binding"; Forbes writes that he "downplayed the risk of bad actors abusing AI and said “we have people who love our country and the world” when asked why there shouldn’t be more formal guardrails and said “no” when a reporter asked him if it requires more than love to protect humans from AI"; and SiliconANGLE (Sep 30) that he "told reporters that the White House is considering forming a 10-person AI safety committee" and "plans to name an “AI czar” by the end of the week". Of Anthropic's chief executive Axios writes: "a MAGA bogeyman and the industry's most prominent advocate for slowing frontier development, signed the pact but stressed to reporters that it was only", in its quotation of him, "a start"; a news agency (Anadolu, Sept 30, 2026) quotes more of what he told reporters after the meeting: "As the president has said, whoever wins AI, wins", and "We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely if we do this right", "If we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safe". The text (the president, by SiliconANGLE, "posted the document on Truth Social late Tuesday"), as Forbes prints it, says each company "should implement the following four layers of controls and audits", in order: "Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways"; "Empower an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated"; "Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended"; and "Designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from the teams operating the controls and the internal and external auditors and evaluators, as well as to ensure any issues identified are remediated"; then: "The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems", and: "Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations". Three of these reports are saved only in versions changed after their first day (Forbes's on Oct 2, SiliconANGLE's on Oct 1 and the trade site Techstrong's on Sept 30, in U.S. Eastern time), so their passages may be newer than that day. Forbes adds that one of Anthropic's people "was seated at the end of the table after months of tension with the White House". Its critics: The Register called it "non-binding and vague regulation" that "doesn’t require them to do anything but does let them set their own rules"; a payments trade site wrote that it "sets no penalties for companies that fall short, and it doesn’t require them to publish audit findings". A trade site (Techstrong) quotes a firm's vice president of strategy and innovation: "Layer three carries the most weight and the least definition. The accord calls for an ‘independent external auditor or evaluator,’ but it does not say who qualifies, what competence they need, what criteria they assess against, or what independence means when an evaluator also sells testing services to the company it assesses". Infosecurity Magazine wrote that its words on models that hack "follows a run of disclosures from three of the signatories": "Anthropic has reported four cases of Claude models accessing third-party systems without authorization after reaching the internet from evaluation environments, while Meta and OpenAI have disclosed testing incidents in which models reached beyond their test environments". A commentary of Oct 13 on the Cato Institute's blog reads the accord both ways. For it: "an innovative approach that provides both the government and industry with the flexibility to adapt to the rapidly evolving capabilities of AI systems", and "making these commitments public could enable federal agencies, such as the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), to step in and punish the labs if they fail to live up to their promises". An earlier public clash over chip-export controls, as CNBC reported it on May 1, 2025. Anthropic had argued in a post of the day before for tighter controls and enforcement ("Maintaining America's compute advantage through export controls is essential for national security and economic prosperity"), saying smugglers had hidden chips in "prosthetic baby bumps" and "packed alongside live lobsters". A Nvidia spokesperson answered: "American firms should focus on innovation and rise to the challenge, rather than tell tall tales that large, heavy, and sensitive electronics are somehow smuggled in" such ways, and: "America cannot manipulate regulators to capture victory in AI"; The Register's update of May 1 gives the first sentence of that reply, which it says Nvidia sent in response to Anthropic's note: "China, with half of the world's AI researchers, has highly capable AI experts at every layer of the AI stack". An Anthropic spokesperson told Fortune: "National security is bigger than the interest of any single company", and that it "stands by its recently filed public submission in support of strong and balanced export controls". That submission, of Apr 29, 2025, says "Anthropic strongly supports" the rule and recommends "export restrictions on certain model weights"; it asks to consider "reducing the number of H100s that Tier 2 countries can purchase without review", and the post of the next day adds two things: "Increase funding for export enforcement", and, for some countries, more chips: "We suggest allowing countries in Tier 2 with robust data center security to obtain more chips", through agreements between governments; its own words are "packing GPUs alongside live lobsters", and its footnote for the baby bumps cites a press report of 2022 about "over 200 Intel Alder Lake CPUs". Anthropic's own pages give its positions through that year: on Mar 6 it advocated "tightening semiconductor export restrictions", "controlling H20 chips" among them; on Jul 23 it wrote that "we are concerned with the Administration's recent reversal on export of the Nvidia H20 chips to China" and urged the administration "to maintain controls on the H20 chip"; on Oct 21 its chief executive wrote that the real risk is "filling the PRC's data centers with US chips they can't make themselves". On Nov 13, 2025 Reuters, relaying the Wall Street Journal, reported that the GAIN AI Act, legislation "to further curb chipmaker Nvidia's ability to export chips to China", "is also backed by AI startup Anthropic", the wire having opened that Amazon "is joining Microsoft in backing legislation" to that end and said that "Microsoft publicly came out in favor of the legislation, while officials at Amazon's cloud unit have privately told Senate staffers that they also support it"; Reuters "could not immediately verify the report", Anthropic did not immediately respond to it, and Nvidia had said the bill "stands to restrict global competition for advanced chips". Five days later Anthropic announced Nvidia's investment in it (the two companies' money line). The same position before and after, from its chief executive's own pages and from reports. A post that his site dates January 2025, of Nvidia's chips in a Chinese laboratory's hands: "H20's are less efficient for training and more efficient for sampling — and are still allowed, although I think they should be banned"; "H100's have been banned under the export controls since their release, so if DeepSeek has any they must have been smuggled (note that Nvidia has stated that DeepSeek's advances are “fully export control compliant”)"; "Well-enforced export controls" "are the only thing that can prevent China from getting millions of chips"; the post says that "A few weeks ago" its author "made the case for stronger US export controls on chips to China" (an op-ed in the Journal, not saved); and of Nvidia itself: "I think the release of the DeepSeek models is clearly not bad for Nvidia"; and the post corrects its author's own earlier count of that laboratory's chips: "It's been reported — we can't be certain it is true — that DeepSeek actually had 50,000 Hopper generation chips", with a note: "In some interviews I said they had “50,000 H100's” which was a subtly incorrect summary of the reporting and which I want to correct here"; the laboratory "is reported to have a mix of all three, adding up to 50,000" (H100, H800 and H20 chips), and "That doesn't change the situation much, but it's worth correcting". An interview published Feb 5, 2025 gives the same advice with its limit: "I would recommend also banning the H20 and attending to making these bans as broad as possible. We always want to be careful — we don’t want to ban other economic activity". TechCrunch (Jan 20, 2026), on his remark at Davos (the company's own line has it from a later recall): the administration had "officially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips, along with a chip line by AMD, to approved Chinese customers"; he said: "I think it would be a big mistake to ship these chips"; TechCrunch notes that "one of those chipmakers, Nvidia, is a major partner and investor in Anthropic", and writes that he "is comparing his partner to an arms dealer". His post of July 27, 2026 on the company's site: "We should not sell powerful chips or chipmaking equipment to China", and "we should crack down on the rampant smuggling". CNBC (Sep 12, 2026) quotes the company's head of public policy: "The government has a critical role to play here, including blocking the sale of the most advanced chips to adversarial nations like China"
The same rule, as other pages of 2025 give each side (the clash of May 1 is on this pair's other context line). Semafor (Mar 2025) recalls that Anthropic's chief executive had said in an interview the month before that the rule was of "less immediate concern to me because it's farther up in the supply chain"; on Apr 29 his company wrote that it "strongly supports" the rule. The Register (May 1, 2025), on the day of Anthropic's post: "Also on Wednesday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just so happened to call on the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on the sale of AI infrastructure outside the US"; "We need to accelerate the diffusion of American AI technology around the world", he said at a press briefing, and "The policies and encouragement from the administration really need to support that"
Its spokesman tells the Times, for the first report: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year". The Times adds that the company "has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China", and that the spokesman said China's government has "blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry". CNBC, that day: it says Huang's interactions with Megaspeed's officials are not unusual and that the chip-diversion allegations about it were "debunked last year". In its statement to several outlets that day: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know"; "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly" (Tom's Hardware); the spokesperson adds, in CNBC's account, that customers do not get access to its trade secrets or to relevant national security information. A spokesperson tells Tom's Guide: "Building American AI infrastructure worldwide has been a core U.S. policy goal of every Administration. Attacking American industry for honoring longstanding U.S. law and policy undercuts national security"; "The PRC government is not seeking NVIDIA products from regional clouds. Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history"; its regional cloud customers receive "ordinary business information" and "zero information relevant to national security". The Times, in its first report: "The company continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner". Bloomberg, on Nov 9: "Today, Megaspeed remains an official Nvidia Cloud Partner", a designation "that Nvidia generally takes away from companies when they no longer do business with those firms"; Reuters, on Nov 10: it "lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner on its directory". Sen. Bennet, in a letter released on Nov 11: "As of October 29, 2026, Nvidia continued to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner"
A spokesman tells the Journal that the photographs of Huang with Alice Huang were taken at meetings that included other Nvidia cloud partners in Asia (the sentence is not in an earlier version of the article, timed Oct 30 in a licensed copy; it is in the version the Journal's page dates Oct 31)
The Financial Times reports that in recent months it "has told cloud computing clients that they must now sell at least 51 per cent of their services to non-Chinese companies", on the word of five people; that the instructions "have been communicated verbally", apply to its clients worldwide and to future contracts only; and, from two people, that it "implemented the new requirement over the summer in a pre-emptive effort to reduce the kind of criticism it routinely receives from US lawmakers and other critics of its approach to China". Its reply in the report: "Data centres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide. Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can. America's longstanding policy has always supported the build-out of American infrastructure worldwide, bringing prosperity, influence and jobs home". The next day a spokesperson, in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation, "did not confirm or deny the verbal requirement", and Invezz relays a follow-up by The Information: the instructions "were intended to encourage a broader customer mix and were not being enforced as a mandatory restriction". Bloomberg, on Nov 6, has it "telling buyers not to rent more than half of their Nvidia computing power to Chinese companies", and writes that the spokesperson "didn't explain the reasoning behind the new Nvidia measure"
The Information reports, as the Daily Caller relays it, that the company "used its influence within the Trump administration to lobby conservative think tanks in Washington", and that one think tank was told its donation was a "tough sell internally" after "a fellow criticized the tech company's relationship with China". The relay names no think tank and gives the lobbying no day. A spokesperson, in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation for its report on OpenAI's silence about chip sales to China: "NVIDIA is the vanguard of America's effort to win the AI race and proud to honor longstanding U.S. policy"; "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide"
Says customer meetings are "part of a CEO's job" and that customers get "zero information relevant to national security"; a spokesman tells the Times Huang "has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed"; the spokesman declines to comment on whether Huang will appear before the committees. In the same statement, to CNBC: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know". PrimeXBT, on Nov 11, gives as from "a statement reported by CNBC on Nov. 5": "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide"; the saved CNBC page of that day does not hold the sentence, which the company gave the Daily Caller News Foundation the day before (its chip of Nov 4)
A spokesman tells the Times the company does not share classified information with its customers, and that customers do not ask it to press the government to change its policies on chip sales to China; China has "consistently promoted its own domestic alternatives in China, including Huawei, and strictly limited imports of our data center products". The Times adds that he "has maintained" that Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were not unusual "and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia's many customers". To the FT, for its report of that day, the company "declined to comment on the government memo and the assertions that its chief executive had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang". The FT adds that the company "has previously said" he meets "thousands of customer executives every year"; NBC's account of Nov 8 gives those words as part of its response to the FT. Two later responses that Bloomberg reports without a day are on the company's chip of Nov 9, the day of Bloomberg's account. Bloomberg reports, as The Edge carries it, that in Southeast Asia it "now requires customers in the region to enrol in its so-called fleet intelligence system", which tracks where participating companies' AI accelerators are, "in order to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners", according to people familiar with the matter; its idea, they say, is "to encourage broader uptake of what remains a voluntary chip tracking programme". The report adds that the system "does not by default require participants to share location data with Nvidia or the US government". Tom's Hardware, relaying the report that day, writes that Nvidia "was not immediately available for comment"; its reply to Bloomberg's questions is on its other chip of that day. A representative tells The National, for its report of that day on the committees' letter, that the company has a robust security team that travels with its chief executive "when needed" and always acts accordingly when the government tells it of entities of concern; the paper says the representative "did not say whether Mr Huang would agree to attend". It prints beside this two sentences of the company's statement of the day before; whether its answers to the paper were a separate exchange the page does not say. Bloomberg reports, as The Edge carries it, that since it "pledged in December 2025 to visit Megaspeed's data centres again in the near future" it "has repeatedly declined to say whether such checks have occurred"; asked "again this week whether Nvidia had conducted any additional checks that would support its CEO's assertions" about counting every processor, "a spokesperson declined to comment"; and it "declined to comment on this question or answer others for this story", the question being whether partners that already hold its cloud-partner label, Megaspeed among them, must enrol in its tracking system; among the others, Bloomberg writes, is "whether the new NCP requirement would be applied in regions beyond Southeast Asia" (the new requirement is on its other chip of that day)
A spokesman tells the Times, for its report on licences for chip sales to Chinese firms: "it makes no sense for the Chinese military to depend on American technology"; Nvidia sells "the first, best and most of our technology in America"; and China has strictly limited imports of the chip
Tells CNBC: "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption" (Business Insider, in a profile stamped early on Nov 9, gives the same two sentences as what "a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday"; its Polish edition repeats them on Nov 10). Tells CBS: "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us". A spokesman tells the Times that Huang will not take part in choosing the outside counsel
Bloomberg reports, about an act of 2025: Nvidia's general counsel "intervened in a US government probe" of Megaspeed, calling a Commerce under secretary in late summer 2025 to ask about it. In Bloomberg's report, as the Business Times of Singapore carries it, a company spokesperson says the general counsel was unaware of the affair when he made the call. Asked by Bloomberg about the company's intervention in the bureau's probe, the spokesperson says that it consults with government officials "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups" (words its spokesman also gives the Times that day: its other chip), and: "Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding US policy and hurt American economic and national security". A spokesman tells the Times the company consults with officials "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions", and works "to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers". At its event in Seoul that day, asked about the investigation and Korea's chip purchases, declines to comment: "Those questions don't seem to be related to today's event"; asked again whether a senior director of the company, whose visit to Korea had been cancelled, had been due to attend, it says "It is difficult for us to comment because" she "was unable to attend" (Asia Economy). A spokesman declines to comment to the Times, which asked on Monday for its report on succession and the board. To the FT it declines to comment on remarks the paper attributes to its general counsel. To Bloomberg Law, for its report of that day on the company's lobbying team, it "declined to comment about its influence team". Reuters's report of that day on the chip bills, in the copy saved, its automated French translation, calls it the main opponent of two of the bills on the word of a former congressional staffer, and says: "Nvidia n'a pas souhaité faire de commentaire" (it did not wish to comment). Just before, the same copy says that until the Justice Department's indictments of the year before "Huang et Nvidia avaient affirmé qu'une telle contrebande n'existait pas" (Huang and Nvidia had maintained that no such smuggling existed), and: "L'entreprise a déclaré qu'elle respectait la législation en matière d'exportation" (the company has said that it complied with export legislation); it gives that statement no day. By the same report an industry council that "compte notamment Nvidia parmi ses membres" (counts Nvidia among its members) "s'est opposé à ces mesures" (opposed the measures), and its spokeswoman "a refusé de commenter la situation actuelle de Nvidia" (refused to comment on Nvidia's present situation). Beside it the report quotes the spokesman of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which it calls a Washington nonprofit "favorable à ces mesures" (in favour of the measures), and to which Open Philanthropy has made awards (the tie lines give them): "L'obstacle que ces projets de loi doivent surmonter est d'obtenir le soutien de la Maison Blanche" (the obstacle these bills must overcome is winning the White House's support), and it would be "coûteux pour la Maison Blanche de soutenir Nvidia dans un bras de fer avec le Congrès" (costly for the White House to back Nvidia in a standoff with Congress). The FT reports, from people familiar with the situation, that its general counsel insisted inside the company the week before that claims of an affair were inaccurate, saying the sources had "an axe to grind with Jensen" and "They are laundering salacious gossip"; what the company told the FT about them is on its other act of that day. In a statement to The National, for its report of that day: "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead", and his tenure would continue "without interruption" (the words of its statement to CNBC the day before). Bloomberg reports, as the Business Times of Singapore carries it, an earlier call: about three months before, its general counsel told a White House official, according to a person familiar with the call, that Alice Huang "is not as important in Megaspeed as she makes herself out to be", and that Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed because of the bad publicity around her. Daring Fireball quotes a Bloomberg report of Dec 22, 2025: Nvidia "told Bloomberg that it went to Megaspeed's facilities multiple times to verify that there's nothing untoward", and a spokesperson said in mid-November 2025: "Our visits confirmed that the GPUs shipped to Megaspeed by our partners are where they are supposed to be". Fortune, listing what it calls "the multiple questionable statements made by Jensen Huang and his company since 2025", recalls two of the company's. In October 2025, when the Times reported that Huang and Alice Huang had been seen drinking together at an industry event, a spokesman said, as the Times printed it then: "Our field operations teams often host groups of customers and partners at conferences, and when Jensen is available, may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market" (Fortune shortens this to "When Jensen is available, [customers] may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market", which makes customers the ones who ask). In December 2025, when Bloomberg reported the investigation of Megaspeed, the company said Megaspeed was "a cloud service permitted under the export control rules"; Bloomberg, recalling that statement on Nov 9, says a spokesperson also said then that the company's own review "had found no evidence of diversion" on Megaspeed's part and showed the firm was "fully owned and operated outside of China, with no China shareholders", and quotes: "When the law is clear, American companies honor US laws as they are, not as America's critics wish they were". CNBC reports, from the company's disclosures, that it spent "a record $2.15 million on federal lobbying in the third quarter", and that its "$4.69 million in 2026 lobbying expenses through September nearly matches the $4.97 million it spent in all of 2025". The totals are for all its federal lobbying; the report ties no sum to a decision. Bloomberg Law, that day, from the same disclosures: the company said it lobbied on issues "related to semiconductor trade policy and artificial intelligence" and on export controls, that it "also disclosed lobbying on quantum computing and energy matters in the third quarter", and that it "lobbied the US Senate and House and executive branch agencies, including the Pentagon, Commerce and Treasury departments, the National Security Council, and others"; beside its in-house lobbyists it retained three outside firms in the third quarter, and a firm it had retained before "filed a termination report effective July 31". ZeroHedge, after listing smuggling charges and reports since and Megaspeed's renting of data-centre capacity to Alibaba, writes that these make "Nvidia's response from last December age like milk", and reprints its own post of Dec 10, 2025 with that response in headline form: "HAVEN'T RECEIVED TIPS OF 'PHANTOM DATACENTERS'", "SMUGGLING SEEMS FARFETCHED", "NVIDIA SAYS IT PURSUES ANY TIPS IT RECEIVES". PC Gamer, on Nov 12, gives the words as the company's answer at the time to the claim that a Chinese model was trained on its Blackwell chips: "While such smuggling seems far-fetched, we pursue any tip we receive". Bloomberg, in an account of that day that Business Standard carries, gives two responses of the company and gives neither a day. It "said in a statement after the Nov. 6 New York Times article" that its cloud partners "do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China", and added: "we trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us" (CBS has that sentence from the company on Nov 8: its chip of that day; the Times's report of Nov 6 has, in the paper's own words, a spokesman's answer to the same effect as the sentence on its cloud partners, that "customers do not ask Nvidia to press the U.S. government to change its policies on chip sales to China": its chip of that day; whether the statement Bloomberg quotes is that answer or a later one is not shown). And: "In response to the Financial Times report about a possible romantic relationship, Nvidia referred to previous comments by Jensen Huang about having a typical business relationship with Alice Huang". Until Nov 17 these stood on the chip of Nov 6
Declines to comment to the Times for its profile of Alice Huang. A spokesperson tells the FT, for its report on the delayed listing of Megaspeed: "we placed Megaspeed on our block list in June 2025, prohibiting any further sales or shipments"; "That voluntary block remains in place". A spokesman tells the Journal, of its general counsel's call to the export bureau: "we have an obligation to resolve any potential 'red flags' before proceeding"; that the ban on sales to Megaspeed is still in place, that Commerce has not blacklisted the company, and that Nvidia got the bureau's permission for parts and replacement components sent since; and that U.S. intelligence officials never gave Huang a warning that he might be a target. Al Jazeera recalls that it welcomed the president's approval, in December 2025, of sales of its H200 chip to China, saying the decision would "support high-paying jobs and manufacturing in America". 24/7 Wall St., as Yahoo Finance carries it, sets beside a short seller's allegation of May, that Chinese demand still drove over 20% of its compute revenue "through illegal diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries", the company's earlier statement: "NVIDIA had said its China compute business went to zero after the April 2025 export restrictions". Axios reports, as Raw Story relays it that day, that some export approvals came before the warning its report describes: "Nvidia disclosed an H200 export license in February". Legal Insurrection quotes Axios's sentence the next day. CNBC recalls that in 2025 it "changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed", and "also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period". The Journal's column of the next evening quotes the filings (the Journal's act of Nov 11). The Information reports on Tuesday, Nov 10, as Gizmodo relays it that day, that Alice Huang's relationship with Huang and the company "helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies since 2023" (the report cites people familiar with the matter). In a statement to The Information, in Gizmodo's words, a spokesperson says the company "primarily sells its data center GPUs through established partners and works with them to ensure compliance with U.S. export controls", "applies the same standards to all transactions", and that "its due diligence and cooperation with law enforcement have helped uncover suspected efforts to evade export restrictions, resulting in federal prosecutions". The Daily Caller News Foundation has the statement in the company's own words the next day (its chip of Nov 11)
Declines to give the Times a statement for its report of a second relationship; declines to comment for another Times article and for an FT report of that day; declines to answer the Journal's questions, for its column of that evening, on where its sales to Megaspeed were classified under its old and new ways of reporting revenue by country, and on whether the end of its separate line for Singapore was related to its block of Megaspeed; and to Politico, for its report of that day on the company's lobbying strategy, as NewsBreak carries it: "Nvidia declined to comment". For the Daily Caller News Foundation's account of The Information's report of the day before, that Alice Huang "used her ties to the Nvidia CEO and the company's distributors to help move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese tech firms since 2023", a spokesperson tells it: "We sell our data-center GPUs primarily to well-known partners", "who work with us to ensure that all sales comply with U.S. export control rules"; "Our due diligence has helped identify suspected attempts to circumvent U.S. export controls, leading to federal prosecutions" (Gizmodo has the statement as given to The Information: its chip of Nov 10). The Wire China, in a profile of Alice Huang published that day: "Jensen Huang is committed to staying on as Nvidia's chief executive, according to a company spokesperson", who added: "America's longstanding policy has always supported the buildout of American infrastructure worldwide, bringing prosperity, influence, and jobs home". The profile gives the statement no day and names no one it was made to; the saved copy was modified on Nov 13. The second sentence stands, spelt "build-out", in the company's reply to the FT of Nov 2 (its chip of that day), and the first matches its statement of Nov 8 that he "is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption"; whether the profile repeats those statements or reports a new one, the page does not say
A spokesperson clarifies, in NBC's report of the resignation, that Huang will not be working with Nvidia in any capacity going forward. The Journal, in another piece of that day, repeats that it "has declined to say how Megaspeed's sales were classified" after it changed how it reports revenue by country (the refusal, to the Journal's column of the evening before, is on its act of Nov 11); Implicator adds that the filings "do not establish a connection between the reporting change and the block". Declines to comment to the FT and the Journal for other reports of that day, and to Reuters for its report that afternoon that Huang "had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter"; Reuters does not name the employee. Tells a nonprofit that found accounts on X defending Huang in what the Washington Post calls an apparent effort that it was aware of the accounts and was trying to identify the source; it did not respond to the Post. TechCrunch's timeline of that day recounts its statements of October 2025, when the investigations of Megaspeed were confirmed: it did not have "any reason to believe products had been diverted", and "NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed - Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules". VentureBeat recalls, in an article on what the resignation means for the financing of AI data centres, its answer to a Reuters investigation of Oct 1 that found lenders wanting stronger guarantees for deals it backs: it "defended its approach, saying outside financing partners independently evaluate customer commitments, anticipated cash flows and equipment resale values". The New York Post, in its report of that day on the Commerce Department, as AOL carries it: it "has been applying immense pressure on Commerce not to impose stricter limits", "putting agency leaders in a bind as they also try to appease China hawks within the administration", according to the chief executive of a research firm, whom the paper names; he gives no occasion. In the same report its spokesperson says that it regularly consults with "BIS, [the Office of Export Enforcement], and other officials to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions, and ask whether they have any follow-ups" (the words it gave the Times and Bloomberg on Nov 9)
Jensen Huang founder and chief executive
Trump gave him the National Medal of Science, Oct 2026; he flew to China on Air Force One, May 2026
Tells Bloomberg, as Taiwan News relays the interview (Bloomberg's saved page shows its opening only): "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual"; as Data Center Knowledge relays it, "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one". Data Center Dynamics has him calling the story "groundless speculation". Quartz relays more of it: "And I think the U.S. government also has as well"; and he said the U.S. government had not told him of its suspicions about her. Yahoo Finance, which carries the Bloomberg report under its reporters' names, has him speak "in an interview Thursday" and say one thing more of her: "She's no longer with Megaspeed, he said". Political.org recalls, in its background to the first report: "in May 2025 Jensen Huang said there was no evidence of any AI chip diversion". SemiAnalysis, on Nov 12, quotes him "at Computex in May 2025": "There's no evidence of any AI chip diversion", and "The important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology"; it sets after the quotation "at least two high profile counter examples". The quotation as it prints it opens with a sentence about counting deployments that Data Center Knowledge gives as from his Bloomberg interview of Oct 29 (his other chip of that day)
Memo to staff: "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife"; "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry"; to his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders: "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility"; on the board's inquiry: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully"; "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence". In the same memo: "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security"; and, as the Times quotes its end: "My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do". Al Jazeera recalls that in August 2025 "the Trump administration announced it would take a 15 percent cut of certain Nvidia chip sales to China"; PC Gamer, the next day: the president "said he'd do it in return for 15% of their China revenue". The Spectator, on Nov 12, recounts the bargain: when the president wanted 20 percent of the revenue from sales of the H20 chip to China, "Huang talked him down to 15"; it quotes the president: "So we negotiated a little deal"
Pulls out of speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum, in TechCrunch's timeline; Business Insider, as The Coin Republic relays it, dates the withdrawal to Nov 9. Wired reports, as TechCrunch and SiliconANGLE relay it that day, that he hired a crisis-communications firm "at least a year before he publicly acknowledged" the relationship; CNBC, Nov 11: the firm he "reportedly hired as early as last year". By the president's account that Monday, tells him by phone that he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy". Apologises to his staff at headquarters that Monday and then runs his meetings "as if it were business as usual", in Fortune's account, which cites CNBC. CNBC, saying the reports "prompted renewed scrutiny" of his past comments on the Chinese market, recalls what he told it on Oct. 22: "No market is closed forever, and China wants foreign companies to invest in China, just as Germany wants foreign companies and countries to invest in Germany"; "There's no reason to believe that market is going to be closed to the best competitors in the world". TechCrunch recalls that he "has publicly lamented export controls", calling them a "failure" at a conference in 2025 and saying in May that it was "not wise" for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems; and that he has warned that shutting Nvidia out of China's market would let the country develop chips to challenge it. Slate, the same day, has him calling the previous administration's policies a failure "that had cost Nvidia and other U.S. companies billions". Emptywheel quotes a news account of the company's gift to the White House ballroom in October 2025: he told reporters at the time that the company was contributing "in a small way" and gave no amount; "Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous". CNN recalls, in an article on whether Nvidia can do without him, that Huang "has said he never believed in succession planning", telling a podcaster earlier in the year "that he hoped to die at his desk". Its live page of Nov 11 gives the remark as a hope to die "on the job", with the reason he gave: the best way, in his view, is "to prepare everyone at the company", passing on "knowledge, information, insight, skills, experience as often and continuously as you can, which is why I continuously reason about everything in front of my team"
Axios reports, as Raw Story relays it that day, among approvals that came before the warning its report describes: he "told Axios in March that the company held licenses covering Chinese customers". Legal Insurrection quotes Axios's sentence the next day
Reached by phone by the Times and asked about a second relationship: "I don't think you should be talking to me directly"; "He then hung up", the Times writes. By Rep. Mast's account to reporters, tentatively agrees that Wednesday night to testify before Congress (CNN). ANI reports, giving no day, that he "addressed the matter during a closed-door staff meeting, expressed regret and did not take questions before moving on to regular business discussions"; Fortune describes an apology to his staff on Monday, Nov 9 (his chip of that day), and the pages do not say whether this is that meeting.
